title: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism
description: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of womenFigure caption, Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equalityByTi
body: How Gloria Steinem changed the lives of generations of womenFigure caption, Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equalityByTiffany WertheimerGloria Steinem was a powerful icon of America's feminist movement and her career spanned numerous roles that changed the lives of generations of women.With her iconic aviator sunglasses and long, blonde-streaked hair - which she considered rebellious in the 1970s - Steinem was an internationally recognised activist in the fight for women's equality.She spoke out for the legalisation of abortion, same-sex marriage, and equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.Her activism was not without a backlash - from both men and women - and harassment that could be as vulgar as it was intimidating.The early yearsBorn on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, Gloria Steinem did not have an easy childhood.Her father Leo Steinem was a travelling salesman and, together with her mother Ruth and older sister Susanne, they lived in a caravan, crisscrossing the country.Leo abandoned the family and moved to California when Steinem was 10 years old, leaving her to care for Ruth who had long suffered with mental illness and had terrifying hallucinations. As a result, Steinem did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gloria Steinem at the 1972 Democratic ConventionShe would later remark that she had never wanted children because she had already had one - her mother.In the late 1950s she went to India on a research scholarship, and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.Steinem left India and moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. It was a time when male-dominated newsrooms made it difficult for women to get hard-hitting stories.Breakthrough articleHer big break came in 1963, when Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny cocktail waitress and wrote A Bunny's Tale, an exposé for Show magazine detailing the seedy and sexist reality of Hugh Hefner's empire.As soon as she arrived for the interview, a security guard called out, "Here bunny, bunny, bunny."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steinem's undercover work as a Playboy Bunny revealed a world of misogyny and exploitationUsing the fake name Marie, she lied about her age - telling Playboy she was 24 years old when she was actually four years older.Steinem lifted the lid on the underpaid life of a Bunny, and the physical pain of wearing the high-heels and tight corsets for hours.Despite the fame - and infamy - that followed, she still found herself struggling to be taken seriously by editors. Though the Playboy exposé helped land her assignments for the New York Times and New York Magazine, often they were about ladies' stockings and the latest hairstyles."To this day when people don't like me they introduce me as a former Bunny, as a put-down," she told the New York Times in 2016. "On the other hand, I did improve the working conditions for those women."All-female journalismUndaunted, by 1968 Steinem was a columnist for New York Magazine, focusing on progressive social issues and women's rights.Her article, After Black Power, Women's Liberation, external brought her national fame, making her the face of the US feminist movement in the 1970s."I was the only woman, and after I wrote an abortion article, my [male] friends there said to me: 'Don't get involved with these crazy women. You've worked hard to be taken seriously,'" she told Rachel Cooke for The Guardian in 2011.So she took matters into her own hands.In 1972, she launched Ms. magazine with a group of feminist activists. It was the first all-female founded and operated periodical, designed to be an alternative to other women's magazines that typically focused on housekeeping and fashion.Image source, EPAImage caption, Ms. magazine broke new ground, selling out within its first week of publicationCritics - mainly men - were quick to write it off. News presenter Harry Reasoner said he gave it six months "before they run out of things to say".The first issue sold out within a week and generated 26,000 subscribers. The magazine is still going today.In 1978, Steinem wrote one of Ms. magazine's most infamous and widely read essays - If Men Could Menstruate. Her satirical reflection on how different power, political and economic structures might be if men had menstrual cycles is still referred to in discussions about gender roles.By the end of her career, Steinem had become a prolific and award-winning writer, penning numerous books including her own memoirs, a biography on Marilyn Monroe and a collection of her own famous quotes in the wryly titled, ‪The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off.Abortion rights campaignerThough still considered one of the world's best-known feminist activists, Steinem came to advocacy rather late in life - in her thirties.At an abortion awareness rally in 1969 where women were sharing their experiences of having abortions, Steinem was encouraged to share her own story about terminating a pregnancy. It had taken place years earlier in London when she was 22 years old, just before going to India.Abortion was illegal in the UK at the time, unless the woman's mental or physical health was in danger. The doctor took a great risk for Steinem, telling her: "You must promise me two things. First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."Nearly 60 years later, Steinem broke one of those promises, when she dedicated her memoir, My Life On The Road, to Dr John Sharpe.She described that abortion speak-out event as a "light bulb moment" - when she realised the US needed a bigger women's rights movement.Almost overnight, Steinem became a crusader for abortion rights, calling it "reproductive freedom". The phrase she coined is credited with making the subject more approachable for political discussion and continues to be used in abortion debates.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Joining Steinem at the 1989 March for Women’s Lives were Susan Sarandon, Gloria Allred, Jesse Jackson and Jane FondaSteinem organised marches and quickly became a draw at demonstrations, although she admitted later that she found talking to the huge crowds "utterly terrifying".After Congress failed to pass the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) in 1970 - legislation granting women equal rights to men - Steinem co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus with fellow feminist leaders and more than 300 women across the US. The group worked to include women in all aspects of political and public life.The same year, she testified at Senate hearings for the ERA, telling the predominantly male audience: "I have been refused service in public restaurants, ordered out of public gathering places and turned away from apartment rentals all for the clearly stated, sole reason that I am a woman."Second-wave feminism continued to gain momentum and Steinem was one of its most famous figureheads.She was also supportive of same-sex marriage, but was criticised for an essay she wrote in 1977 on transgender people. She clarified her position in 2013, saying the words in her "old essay" had been taken "out of time and context"."I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned," she wrote in an opinion piece, external.Steinem was also criticised for a 1998 essay in the New York Times, where she showed support for then-President Bill Clinton after news broke of his scandalous affair with intern Monica Lewinsky - who was 22 years old at the time."The truth is that even if the allegations are true, the president is not guilty of sexual harassment," Steinem wrote. "He is accused of having made a gross, dumb and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life."In 2017, she said she "wouldn't write the same thing now".Too glamorous?Critics came from the left as well as right, targeting Steinem for everything from her looks to her motives. Some claimed she was too glamorous to be a true feminist, while others said she was successful only because of her appearance.Betty Friedan, author of The Feminine Mystique, the book credited with launching second-wave feminism, was annoyed that Steinem became the face of the movement, accusing her of "ripping off the movement for private profit" when she launched Ms.The media were trying "to make her a celebrity," fumed Friedan, "but no one should mistake her for a leader."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steinem's sudden rise to become the face of second-wave feminism caught the ire of some activistsUS President Richard Nixon was recorded during a secret conversation furiously ranting about Steinem, to which she responded: "There is some opinion that Richard Nixon is the most sexually insecure chief of state since Napoleon".Al Goldstein, the notorious pornographer and publisher of Screw magazine, launched a campaign of attacks that included publishing her phone number next to fake advertisements for oral sex.He also printed a graphic centrefold image of a Steinem look-alike, and hung it open on display at the newsstand outside Ms. magazine's office building. She had to look at it every day.As she got older, harassment to this degree became less common. However, given she was a recognisable figure in New York City, it was not uncommon for Steinem to be stopped on the street by strangers wanting to debate - sometimes with an edge of hostility.But she welcomed the continued debate. In 2020, she was among a cross-section of public figures who signed an open letter denouncing cancel culture, saying it weakens open debate by shutting people down."If you care about having the conversation, surely you want to try in a humane way to convince the other person, not do away with them," she told the New York Times.'I can't mate in captivity'Gloria Steinem once quipped: "I can't mate in captivity" - a reference to her disinterest in marriage. But she publicly enjoyed a healthy dating life with a number of rich and famous bachelors, giving critics more ammunition to use against her.They included Frank Thomas who was head of the Ford Foundation; film director Mike Nichols and Olympic decathlete Rafer Johnson (who helped tackle the man who assassinated Robert F Kennedy in 1968)."I was the one always accused of using men, of being too sexual. Someone once sent me a cartoon of a tombstone that said 'at last she sleeps alone'," she wrote.But in 2000, aged 66, she wed David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist, and father of actor Christian Bale.At the time, the union drew gasps of surprise and even disappointment from some feminists, who had spent years following Steinem's heated debates surrounding marriage laws.But she said those laws had finally changed. "If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights. That's not true anymore. It's possible to make an equal marriage," she explained years later.Steinem also confessed to it being a "green card marriage" because Bale's US visa was running out - but said that they loved each other and were going to be together regardless.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, David Bale and Gloria Steinem, pictured with Maurine RothschildBale died three years later from brain lymphoma.Steinem had her own health scare with breast cancer in 1986, and underwent a lumpectomy.'So much to do'Gloria Steinem once said she wanted to live to 100 because "there's so much to do".In her near-century of life, she even became a talented tap dancer.She was given America's highest civilian honour - the Presidential Medal of Freedom - in 2013 by President Barack Obama, who credited her work with giving more women "the respect and opportunities that they deserve".In 2024, she reached the age of 90. She lived alone in New York, content in the knowledge that Ms. Magazine was still publishing.Steinem seized the occasion to tell the BBC that she hoped her legacy "might help individual people... to become more the unique, valuable, loved and lovable person that they want to be."She will be remembered for amplifying the voices of women in a way that mainstream media at the time either could not, or would not.And, in so doing, she altered the landscape and language of women's rights in America.

schema.headline: Gloria Steinem: An icon of American feminism

title: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says
description: "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram."I instruc
body: "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram."I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response."Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building.Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses"."Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added.Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices.A nearby café was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike.Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third café to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion."Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added.The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa.In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets.In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack.

schema.headline: Russian drone hits Ukranian security headquarters, Zelensky says

title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
description: The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.The distortio
body: The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made. The Mercator map shows the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing bigger.In an effort to correct this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, saying it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency: "A fair world begins with a fair map."Earlier he had told a UN briefing: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."The UN vote is non-binding but will see changes to the maps used by institutions around the world.

schema.headline: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size

title: Gloria Steinem: Feminist activist and journalist dies, aged 92
description: Gloria Steinem, who became a leader of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died aged 92. In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "p
body: Gloria Steinem, who became a leader of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died aged 92. In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City on Wednesday, "surrounded by many who loved her". Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance - a group dedicated to fighting sexism - more than 50 years ago.She started her career as a journalist in New York and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on women's issues other than housekeeping and beauty.During the 1970s, Steinem was a vocal campaigner for women's reproductive rights, among other causes.She herself obtained an illegal abortion in London when she was 22 years old, and years later celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.She also spoke out in favour of the legalisation of same-sex marriage, as well as equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, she had a difficult childhood and did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.After university in the late 1950s, she went to India on a research scholarship and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.She then moved to New York City in the early 1960s to start her career as a freelance writer. Her big break came through an exposé of Playboy Bunny working conditions. Eventually she became a columnist for New York Magazine, before founding Ms. magazine in 1972. For years, Steinem famously eschewed marriage, but she went on to tie the knot in 2000 to David Bale, a South African-born entrepreneur-environmentalist and father of actor Christian Bale. He died three years later from brain lymphoma.When questioned over why she changed her position on marriage, she replied: "I didn't change. Marriage changed."In 2013, then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honour in the US.Her foundation said "she continued working for equality until the very end"."Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour."Her foundation said she lived her last years being in community and writing - welcoming guests into her home for "Talking Circles" - a tradition that will continue.Her commitment to her home becoming a centre for social justice movements, and a forthcoming book An Unexpected Life, are "among many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come", the foundation said.Tributes flowed on Thursday after the news of her death, with writers and feminists commenting on Instagram with gratitude, some of them saying she had changed their lives.Meghan Markle "celebrated the life and legacy of my friend and mentor", along with pictures of the pair on Instagram."You all know her many accolades and the way in which she helped shape the world for woman and all people", Markle said, but added that beyond their work together, Steinem "privately, was even better than you would imagine".Steinem spent Thanksgiving with Markle's family, introduced the younger woman to one of her best friends, loved "our children with her whole heart, counseling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivaled cheekiness and wit", she said.Markle now wears "with pride" a bracelet Steinem gave her that says "we are linked, not ranked".Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and 2016 presidential candidate said Steinem was "one of the architects of the entire structure of women's equality, I mean tearing down those obstacles to young women being able to participate where their talents and hard work took them"."Gloria was at heart an optimist," Clinton told CBS Mornings on Thursday. "Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that's a moral choice, and she made it every day."

schema.headline: Gloria Steinem: Feminist activist and journalist dies, aged 92

title: Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
description: The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of the biggest restructuring in the group's almost nin
body: The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of the biggest restructuring in the group's almost nine-decade history. It brings the total number of roles the carmaker plans to shed by 2030 to 100,000, after announcing in March that it would cut 50,000 roles.The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - is also considering the future of four of its German plants.The move is a "strong signal" for the future of the firm, which is "taking responsibility for our entire workforce", VW's chief executive Oliver Blume said in a statement on Thursday.Blume said in July that the firm was looking to make the additional cuts.Shares in the company were up by around 7% in Frankfurt on Friday morning.The Golf-maker has been hit by a drop in profits due to falling sales and fierce competition, especially from Chinese brands.The firm also said that by 2035 it would cut the number of models it produces by 50% and reduce the complexity of its offering by 75%.VW will also prioritise the "most compelling vehicles" and make more of each model, which will help lower costs, it said.A "fundamental adjustment of the global workforce capability is necessary" to safeguard the competitiveness of the company, which faces shifting demand and technological change.It added "a group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions - including management roles - will be necessary."The company is also weighing options for operations in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm, where it has said production capacity exceeds demand."Alternative uses for these plants are being assessed," it said.As of 2025, VW employed more than 660,000 people worldwide. Its brands also include Seat, Bentley and Lamborghini.Christianne Benner - the president of Europe's largest industrial union IG Metall and deputy chair of VW's Supervisory Board - said the carmaker had "fought hard for good solutions" to address a "crisis situation".VW's profits have fallen sharply in recent years, hit by falling sales in China, which was once one of its biggest markets.Sales have also fallen in the US, partly due to the impact of tariffs on car imports that were introduced by President Donald Trump's administration.Chinese carmakers have been expanding aggressively as they roll out new technologies while benefiting from lower production costs than their rivals.In recent years, firms such as BYD have seen their sales rise sharply in markets including the UK, European Union and South East Asia.

schema.headline: Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs

title: Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv
description: US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, as efforts to end the war appear to be gathering pace.Ukrai
body: US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, as efforts to end the war appear to be gathering pace.Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed he will meet with the envoys on Sunday, after they visit Moscow on Saturday to hold talks with meet Russian President Vladimir Putin.Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, but a gulf remains between the two warring sides. Earlier on Friday, Zelensky said a Russian drone hit the office of Ukraine's security chief Oleksandr Poklad in Kyiv. Poklad appears to be unharmed. In a post on social media, Zelensky said he had ordered Poklad, who head the SBU security service, to respond "adequately" to the attack.Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Russia multiple times, but the purported talks will be the first in Ukraine.Zelensky said he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.Russia's state news agency Tass said Witkoff and Kushner were "expected to arrive in Moscow and then to Kyiv... on 5-6 September", quoting a source.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later told reporters: "I wouldn't announce anything, but when these contacts take place, we will inform you."Meanwhile, Putin told an international economic forum on Thursday that "there are chances" a peace deal could be reached."First of all, Moscow and Kyiv must agree between themselves," he said.But he showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine.Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly rejected Putin's terms saying they are tantamount to capitulation. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and currently controls about 20% of its territory.

schema.headline: Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv

title: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
description: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tu
body: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tunnelByTessa WongAsia Digital ReporterA tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border."It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people."I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors."We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said. He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water. Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers found a substantial amount of water in the tunnel as they dug through itFinally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay". Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone'Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers."Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time. "It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located. "We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers had to pull the survivors through a tiny passageway created at the top of the rubble in the tunnel

schema.headline: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel

title: US billionaire Leon Black defies summons and sues Epstein panel
description: Billionaire investor Leon Black has failed to appear before a US congressional committee investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein - instead
body: Billionaire investor Leon Black has failed to appear before a US congressional committee investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein - instead filing a lawsuit challenging the committee's efforts to summon him.The lawsuit calls the subpoenas issued by the House Oversight Committee "invalid" and says they hold "no legitimate connection" to the committee's legislative aim.Black walked out of the committee in June while giving voluntary testimony after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time. Black has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein. The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June. His lawsuit opposing these summonses, which was filed in federal court in Washington on Thursday, argued that revealing the NDAs might "expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it". NDAs are contracts where both parties agree to keep information confidential, often as part of a settlement or employment agreement."This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black," Susan Estrich, an attorney for Black, said in a press release on Thursday."We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power." "By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two Congressional subpoenas," Robert Garcia, who sits on the committee, said in a statement after Black failed to appear. "His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable. We must hold him in contempt immediately," Garcia added.Contempt of Congress could result in the committee referring Black to the justice department for potential prosecution."It's a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people," Chairman Jomes Comer said. "Mr Black's testimony is crucial to our investigation."Black has said he employed Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling the House Oversight Committee in June that he had paid Epstein $158m (£120m) for legitimate purposes over the course of their years-long association.He has said he did not know about Epstein's "nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019". Black appears in the Epstein files released by the justice department, which include photos, videos and investigative documents relating to the disgraced late financier. There is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.Black had a six-year affair with a former Russian model, Guzel Ganieva, which ended in allegations of abuse, court records show.According to a lawsuit filed by Ganieva against Black, which was later dismissed, he prepared a nondisclosure agreement in 2015 to secure her silence.Epstein offered Black advice, including suggesting in an email to his assistant that Black hire former law enforcement officers to approach Ganieva, according to files released by the US justice department.Estrich, Black's attorney, has dismissed Ganieva's accusation as "demonstrably false". Black himself has previously said he was the victim of extortion.A judge ultimately dismissed Ganieva's lawsuit, citing the NDA she signed and about $9m (£6.6m) that she had received in the years after entering the agreement.Black left Apollo Global Management, a company he co-founded, in 2021 - saying at the time that "relentless public attention and media scrutiny" of his ties with Epstein had taken "a toll" on his health.

schema.headline: US billionaire Leon Black defies summons and sues Epstein panel

title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
description: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic object
body: Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DCThe problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of stasis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, LondonI do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to IranThe latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.What is the White House's exit strategy? Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

schema.headline: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views

title: Pig kidney works in human body for 271 days - is this the future of organ transplants?
description: A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.Tim Andrews said the transplant gave
body: A kidney transplanted from a pig has worked inside a patient for 271 days – the longest on record, say US doctors.Tim Andrews said the transplant gave him "hope" and spared him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine.The team at Mass General Brigham hospital say their work shows pig organs can be used as a "bridge" until a human transplant becomes available.But the pig organ eventually failed and was removed so Andrews needed a short bout of dialysis before a donor was found.Doctors and scientists are exploring xenotransplantation – using organs from other species – due to shortages of organs for transplants.In the US, around 100,000 people are waiting for a kidney while only 25,000 transplants occur each year. More than 7,000 people in the UK are on the kidney transplant list. Andrews was told it could take seven years to get to the top of the list, but that people live only five years, on average, on dialysis."I had a little bit of a shortage of time… it becomes very depressing," he said.But he described the idea of a pig transplant as "hope" and the "light at the end of the tunnel"."Hope is the biggest thing, the chance to be free from the [dialysis] machine and live your life."

schema.headline: Pig kidney works in human body for 271 days - is this the future of organ transplants?

title: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims
description: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Br
body: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.When asked about if the prime minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said "they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish"."Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory."The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government." The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.  The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas."That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable"."Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands. "We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies". "If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others." Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

schema.headline: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims

title: South Africa's Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice and compensation
description: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville ByPumza FihlaniReporting fromSharpevilleAbraham Mofokeng still
body: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville ByPumza FihlaniReporting fromSharpevilleAbraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg."We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government."All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.Mofokeng is now part of a legal case announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling. The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.Image source, Universal History Archive/UIG via Getty imagesImage caption, Protesters started fleeing as the police opened fireSharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng."The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest."[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.Image caption, Lazarus Magotsi witnessed police shooting at some who were trying to get up from the groundAnother survivor, Lazarus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself."We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says."People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them."Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.Image source, Universal History Archive/UIG via Getty imagesImage caption, The photographer Ian Berry later told the BBC that it seemed the man in the centre of this picture was holding his jacket up "as though to protect himself from the bullets"The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994."Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive."Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past"."Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen."So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".Image caption, Many of those who died in the massacre are buried in a long row in a cemetery in SharpevilleThe TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma."Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng."Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

schema.headline: South Africa's Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice and compensation

title: US investigating if missile hit Iran wedding, Vance says
description: Figure caption, Watch: JD Vance "extremely sceptical" over alleged strike on Iranian weddingByDan SalesThe US military is investigating Iranian claims
body: Figure caption, Watch: JD Vance "extremely sceptical" over alleged strike on Iranian weddingByDan SalesThe US military is investigating Iranian claims that its strikes killed at least four people including two children at a wedding in southern Iran, Vice-President JD Vance has said.The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) - a humanitarian group - said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony at a home in Sirik on Tuesday, prompting Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei to declare it a "war crime".US missiles were fired the same day over "attempted attacks" by Iran on American forces, but a US Central Command spokesperson said it "never targets civilians".Speaking on Thursday, Vance said he was "extremely sceptical" over reports of the alleged strike but confirmed the US would investigate."I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far. So I'm extremely sceptical of this," Vance told a White House briefing. "I know that we're investigating." Iran has launched fresh attacks on US bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates in response to the alleged strike. The IRCS said 67 people were hurt when shrapnel from the missile hit a family wedding ceremony, killing at least four people. Iranian state media said a fifth person, a woman aged 22, had died in hospital shortly after.The four people killed were named locally as Zarkhatoon Taheri, 50; Kolsum Mallahi Nazhdnia, 43; Mohammad Mallahi, 16; and Amirali Karimi, four.Image source, Iranian Red Crescent SocietyImage caption, A picture distributed by the Iranian Red Crescent Society purportedly showing the remains of a building which was hosting the wedding ceremonyBBC Verify confirmed a video and two images taken on Tuesday near Kuhestak's coast that showed a telecommunications tower being destroyed, and other videos from Tuesday and Wednesday showed severely damaged houses about 130m (427ft) north of the tower.BBC Persian Forensics found the telecommunications tower was about 112m (367 ft) from the house where the wedding was being held.Fighting with Iran has continued for over half a year since the US and Israel launched a joint attack on the country on 28 February.

schema.headline: US investigating if missile hit Iran wedding, Vance says

title: Argentine couple to return Nazi-looted painting to rightful owner
description: A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has
body: A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has ruled. The late-baroque Portrait of a Lady was lost for 80 years until it was spotted in photographs of a house for sale near Buenos Aires.The house belonged to Patricia Kadgien, the daughter of a Nazi fugitive who had fled there after the Second World War, and she has now agreed to return the painting in exchange for not being prosecuted for concealing it from the authorities.Portrait of a Lady was among over 1,000 artworks looted from the collection of Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940.His daughter-in-law and sole heir Marei von Saher intends for the painting to be exhibited on a temporary loan at the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires to spread awareness of the issue, Argentine newspaper Clarin reports.Von Saher has previously said her family "aims to bring back every single artwork robbed from Jacques' collection, and to restore his legacy".This painting was first recognised in August 2025 by the Dutch Algemeen Dagblad (AD) newspaper on an estate agent's website of a property in the coastal town of Mar del Plata.It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father Friedrich Kadgien had been a top adviser to Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's deputy. Goring plundered thousands of works across Europe.

schema.headline: Argentine couple to return Nazi-looted painting to rightful owner

title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah R
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoAs summer temperatures in Europe smashed records and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.Poland's interior minister is clear."There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.August campaign across Europe4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a warehouse of defence firm EMCO in Tryavna. In a statement, the company recalled previous blasts at its facilities which were investigated for links to Russia. "Human error is excluded," it said.13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion. The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires. One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out". An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.Separately, police say they are hunting a climate extremist suspected of sabotage attacks this week on power substations in western Germany.Image source, EPAImage caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firmsWhy is this happening now?Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.The novelty now is the concentration of cases."The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine."We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes. After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.There are other theories.To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses."Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe."They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland. One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.Who are the suspected saboteurs?Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.That would be unusual.The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.Nato faced with Soviet-style campaignRussia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war."I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

schema.headline: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
